endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Use digital content transparency solutions to enable the documentation of each instance where content is generated, modified, or shared to provide a tamperproof history of the content, promote transparency, and enable traceability.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether assessing awareness of AI feedback and reporting channels increases their use or improves safety, and no supplied study documents the hazard of unused channels. The one endorsement comes from a NIST framework whose quoted text addresses content provenance and traceability rather than awareness of feedback channels.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The recommendation currently rests on a single framework endorsement and on reasoning about how feedback systems work, not on observed outcomes.

NIST AI 600-1 is a voluntary framework, and its quoted language uses "should." The passage calls for documenting when content is generated, modified, or shared so that history can be traced. That supports transparency in general terms, but it does not directly instruct organizations to measure whether patients or communities know that reporting channels exist.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that measure baseline awareness of AI feedback channels among patients, clinicians, and community members, then test whether awareness assessments and the outreach they prompt change reporting volume, report quality, and the time it takes to detect AI-related errors. Such studies should report results separately by language, literacy level, and insurance type.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested this practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. These groups may be least likely to learn about reporting channels through standard notices, and the absence of data means health systems cannot tell whether awareness efforts reach them.
